title: Input Handling
summary: Raw input (keys, mouse buttons, gamepad sticks) is not what game code should depend on. Engines turn it into **actions** ("jump", "move left"), track for each one whether it was **pressed**, **held** or **released** this frame, and let players **rebind** the keys. This lesson builds that layer, and covers gamepads, dead zones and input buffering.
markdown:
## From devices to actions Game code should never ask "is the space bar down?". It should ask "does the player want to jump?". The difference matters as soon as you support rebinding, a gamepad, or a second keyboard layout: ```mermaid flowchart LR K["Keyboard
Space, W, A, D"] --> B["Bindings
Space → Jump
W → MoveUp
Pad A → Jump"] P["Gamepad
A button, left stick"] --> B M["Mouse"] --> B B --> S["Action state this frame
Jump: pressed
MoveUp: held"] S --> G["Game code
if (input.pressed(Action::Jump))"] ``` ## Pressed, held and released Lesson 5.07 showed two ways to read keys: messages, and the current state. For game controls the cleanest model is: once per frame, take a **snapshot** of every action's state (down or up), and keep the previous frame's snapshot. Then for each action: | Query | Previous | Now | Use for | |---|---|---|---| | `held` | (any) | down | Continuous actions: walking, aiming, charging | | `pressed` | up | down | One-shot actions: jump, fire one shot, open a menu | | `released` | down | up | Releasing a charged attack, ending a drag | Because the snapshot is taken once at the start of the frame (lesson 10.01's input phase), every system in that frame sees the same answer. Checking the live key state in the middle of an update lets two systems disagree about whether a key was pressed. There is one trap: a tap shorter than a frame can be **missed** by pure polling, because the key is already up again when the snapshot is taken. Recording "went down at least once this frame" from the key-down messages, as well as the current state, fixes it. ## Bindings and rebinding A **binding** maps a physical input to an action. Keep them in data, not code: ```cpp enum class Action { MoveLeft, MoveRight, Jump, Attack, Count }; struct Binding { int key; Action action; }; std::vector bindings{ { 'A', Action::MoveLeft }, { VK_LEFT, Action::MoveLeft }, { 'D', Action::MoveRight }, { VK_RIGHT, Action::MoveRight }, { VK_SPACE, Action::Jump }, { 'J', Action::Attack }, }; ``` Several keys may map to one action (an action is down if **any** of its keys is down). Rebinding is then just editing the table and saving it with the settings (lesson 10.07). Use virtual-key codes or, for layout-independent positions such as WASD, scan codes (lesson 5.07). ## Gamepads and dead zones On Windows, Xbox-compatible controllers are read with **XInput** (`XInputGetState`) or the newer GameInput API; libraries like SDL (chapter 11) cover many controllers. Analogue sticks report numbers (for XInput, −32768 to 32767 per axis), and a stick at rest never reads exactly zero: it drifts by a few percent. A **dead zone** ignores small values: ```cpp float applyDeadZone(float value, float deadZone) // value from -1 to 1 { const float magnitude{ std::abs(value) }; if (magnitude < deadZone) return 0.0f; // Rescale so movement starts smoothly from 0 just outside the dead zone. return std::copysign((magnitude - deadZone) / (1.0f - deadZone), value); } ``` For a 2D stick, apply the dead zone to the length of the (x, y) vector, not each axis separately, or diagonal movement feels wrong. ## Input buffering Players press buttons slightly early. If the jump button was pressed three frames before the character landed, a strict game ignores it and the player feels the game "ate" their input. **Buffering** remembers recent presses for a short window (often 100 to 150 ms) and acts on them as soon as the action becomes possible. Its cousin, **coyote time**, still allows a jump for a few frames after walking off a ledge. Small touches like these are a large part of why some games "feel" responsive. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Hard-coding keys in game logic > Map keys to actions in one place, so rebinding and gamepads work everywhere. > [!warning] Reading live key state during the update > Snapshot once per frame so every system agrees. > [!warning] No dead zone on analogue sticks > Characters drift on their own. Apply a dead zone to the stick vector. > [!warning] Acting on input while the window is unfocused > `GetAsyncKeyState` sees keys typed in other programs. Ignore input when the game is not in front. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why should game code use actions rather than keys? + So controls can be rebound and gamepads work unchanged - Because reading keys directly is slower - Because Windows does not report which key was pressed - So that input can only be read once per frame > Game code asks "is Jump pressed?", and the binding table decides which keys or buttons mean Jump. ? How are pressed and released worked out? - From how long the key has been held + By comparing this frame's state with last frame's - From the number of key-down messages received this frame - By asking the operating system for the key's repeat count > Keeping last frame's snapshot is all it takes; "held" is simply down in this frame. ? Why apply a 2D stick's dead zone to its length rather than to each axis? + Because per-axis dead zones distort diagonal directions and make movement snap to the axes - Because the length is cheaper to compute than two axes - Because each axis already has a dead zone built into the hardware - Because gamepads report only one axis at a time > A radial dead zone ignores small movements in every direction equally. ? An action was up last frame and is down now. Which queries are true? - Only `released` - Only `held` + `pressed` and `held` > Pressed is the transition; held is the current state. ? Why take one input snapshot per frame? + So every system in that frame sees the same input state - To save memory - Because keys can only be read once > Mixing live reads makes systems disagree. ? What is a dead zone for? - Disabling input during loading screens + Ignoring a resting stick's small readings - Making buttons harder to press > Without it, characters creep around on their own. ? What does input buffering do? - Stores all input for replays - Delays input to make the game harder + Remembers a press until the action is possible > It forgives presses that come slightly early. ```
ideas:
- Add a binding table and pressed/held/released tracking to lesson 5.06's program, and make the square jump only on `pressed`.
- Read an Xbox controller with `XInputGetState` and print the left stick with and without a dead zone.
- Implement a 120 ms jump buffer and feel the difference.

cards.q: Why should game code use actions rather than keys?
cards.a:
So controls can be rebound and gamepads work unchanged

Game code asks "is Jump pressed?", and the binding table decides which keys or buttons mean Jump.

cards.q: How are pressed and released worked out?
cards.a:
By comparing this frame's state with last frame's

Keeping last frame's snapshot is all it takes; "held" is simply down in this frame.

cards.q: Why apply a 2D stick's dead zone to its length rather than to each axis?
cards.a:
Because per-axis dead zones distort diagonal directions and make movement snap to the axes

A radial dead zone ignores small movements in every direction equally.

cards.q: An action was up last frame and is down now. Which queries are true?
cards.a:
`pressed` and `held`

Pressed is the transition; held is the current state.

cards.q: Why take one input snapshot per frame?
cards.a:
So every system in that frame sees the same input state

Mixing live reads makes systems disagree.

cards.q: What is a dead zone for?
cards.a:
Ignoring a resting stick's small readings

Without it, characters creep around on their own.

Remembers a press until the action is possible

It forgives presses that come slightly early.
